items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: So when I got up to play for Ted Fio Rito, he offered me a job right there.

ctx.x: Well you went through a real succession of great big bands and you must have been popular, because you hit them all.

I was very fortunate. Back home, when I was fourteen, fifteen, sixteen years old, there used to be a couple of places, one in Moline and one in Davenport, where all the big bands came to play the big ballrooms. The Coliseum in Davenport in particular, and every time a band like Ted Weems or Harry James or Ted Fio Rito, I’m naming some of the old guys now, all the kids would say “hey, let Louie play the drums” you know. So the band leader would always say “yeah, okay, where is he?” And I’d get up and I’d play you…
You were what, seventeen or something?

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That set was made – the first band was Ted FioRito. I had that when I was working with Ted FioRito for six months, before I joined Benny.

ctx.x: Went did you actually have your first double-bass-drum kit? You already came up with the prototype in 1938. You had already started designing it. So when did you actually have one?

That set was made – the first band was Ted FioRito. I had that when I was working with Ted FioRito for six months, before I joined Benny. That was an oddity. I took up half the bandstand with that kit.
And it’s all your own design, especially with that large tom in the middle? That’s all your design?
